What Can Be Learned About Frontend Performance?

Applying structured debugging techniques and the right tools significantly improved the performance of our Vue.js application. Our main lessons were to profile before optimising, to use Chrome DevTools and APM tools for insight, and to use VueUse utilities to handle common cleanup problems.

Common frontend performance pitfalls ✅:

  • Unoptimised WebSocket or API calls.
  • Memory leaks due to lingering intervals or event listeners.
  • Inefficient rendering due to excessive state updates.

Tools that helped 🛠:

  • Chrome DevTools for profiling and debugging.
  • APM tools (RUM.js) for real-time performance monitoring.
  • VueUse utilities (useIntervalFn, useEventListener) to handle common issues efficiently.

Key takeaways 🔹:

  • Always profile your application before optimising.
  • Use Chrome DevTools and APM tools to gain insights.
  • Avoid common pitfalls like uncleared intervals and dangling event listeners.
  • Leverage VueUse utilities for better state management and cleanup.

Performance tuning is an iterative process that requires a deep understanding of your application’s behaviour. By using the right tools and following best practices, developers can efficiently diagnose and resolve frontend performance issues.

We hope this case study provides valuable insights into Vue.js performance tuning for fresh graduates and new developers. 🚀

Happy coding!

FAQ

How do I know if my Vue.js App has a memory leak?

Taking Titansoft’s Front-End Project as an example, the warning signs were browsers freezing after 10–15 minutes of use, input lag that grew after navigating through multiple pages, and memory and CPU usage that climbed as components were remounted. The Memory tab in Chrome DevTools detects memory leaks and excessive memory usage. We traced our leaks to uncleared setInterval timers and event listeners that were never removed.

How to start Vue.js performance tuning?

Start by profiling your application before you optimise anything. Our team at Titansoft used Chrome DevTools to profile and debug, and RUM.js (Elastic APM) to monitor performance in real time. We then applied fixes such as useIntervalFn and useEventListener. Performance tuning is an iterative process that depends on understanding how your application behaves.

Hey Vue developers 👋

I’ve been building `vue-pdf-export`, an open-source Vue 3 + TypeScript library for generating PDFs directly in the browser.

I started this project because I kept rebuilding the same PDF features across Vue applications: pagination, preview, printing, headers, footers, progress tracking, and long-document support. I wanted a reusable component and composable rather than repeating that infrastructure in every project.

**In short:** Generate PDFs from Vue 3 components in the browser using either Canvas rendering or selectable, searchable text. The package also supports smart pagination, tables, headers, footers, watermarks, preview, download, print, and SSR-safe imports for Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4.

You can explore the actual PDF output without setting up a project:

Here is what the published package supports:

> **Quick answer — How do I generate a PDF in Vue 3?** Install `vue-pdf-export`, import `Html2Pdf` and its stylesheet, place your document in the `#pdf-content` slot, and call `generatePdf()` from a Vue template ref. Use `render-mode=”text”` for native searchable/selectable body text; choose `render-mode=”canvas”` when complex browser CSS fidelity matters most. Both modes generate PDFs in the browser.

## Features

- **Powerful:** choose Canvas or selectable-text output, use your own Vue document components, and control page breaks.
- **Modular:** use the component or composable, and add only the slots and options your document needs. PDF engines load when generation runs.
- **Customizable:** style exported content with your CSS and export-only options; theme the built-in preview and loader with CSS variables.
- Canvas and selectable-text PDF rendering
- Smart automatic/manual pagination, keep-together blocks and container-aware splitting
- Explicit page breaks, repeated table headers and opt-in pagination diagnostics
- Preview, download, and native browser print
- Blob, ArrayBuffer, Base64, and PDF data-URL output
- Header/footer object options, Vue slots and page targeting
- PDF composition: prepend or append existing PDF pages
- Standard paper formats and custom dimensions in portrait or landscape
- Text, image and trusted HTML watermarks with optional design presets; text marks use reusable vector outlines instead of selectable PDF text
- Password protection, permissions, metadata, and compression
- Clickable PDF links
- Progress reporting, generation metrics, and cancellation
- `data-pdf-ignore` for export-only DOM control
- PDF-only page/body styling and custom CSS
- Large-document rendering optimizations
- Font readiness, optional TTF/TrueType-outline OTF embedding, chart snapshots and SVG fallback
- Opt-in image optimization with explicit quality controls and per-export asset reuse metrics
- Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4 SSR-safe imports
- TypeScript declarations
- npm, pnpm, Yarn, Yarn PnP, and Bun consumer validation

For detailed API options, examples, renderer notes, styling, pagination,
security, SSR guidance, and production recommendations, see the
**full documentation**.

> **Security note:** Header, footer, and slot HTML is sanitized before entering export staging. Treat caller-provided HTML as untrusted and apply your application’s input validation policy.

> **Privacy and network boundary:** Ordinary PDF generation happens in your browser and does not upload document content to a package-operated server. URL-based templates, remote fonts/images, and external export stylesheets may still be fetched from their configured origins.

## Complete Vue 3 PDF generation guide

> **Scope:** This guide describes the currently published `vue-pdf-export` functionality and combines practical examples with API detail. Code samples and recorded benchmarks reflect the documented test scenarios; run your own target-browser tests before shipping production PDFs. For the maintained source of truth, use the official documentation and GitHub repository.

This complete technical guide covers installation, JavaScript and TypeScript usage, components and composables, rendering modes, pagination, styling, page layers, programmatic output, performance, testing, production checks, and browser limitations. It also links to the detailed performance engineering report for reproducible measurements.

## Get Started

### Introduction

`vue-pdf-export` is a Vue 3 HTML-to-PDF component and composable for browser applications. Use it from JavaScript or TypeScript.

The API includes smart split controls, row-aware tables, header/footer objects and Vue slots, PDF composition, expanded paper sizes, font readiness, chart snapshots, SVG fallback, and opt-in image optimization.

It supports two rendering modes:

- **Canvas mode** — maximum HTML/CSS visual fidelity through `html2pdf.js` + `html2canvas` + `jsPDF`.
- **Selectable text mode** — browser-side vector PDF rendering with real selectable/searchable/copyable text, clickable PDF links, password protection, metadata, compression, page-aware headers/footers, and watermarks.

It also includes manual and automatic pagination, preview, download, native browser print, Blob/ArrayBuffer/Base64 output, export-only page/body styling, `data-pdf-ignore`, custom export CSS, external print stylesheets, forced light/dark themes, width auto-fit, safe filename normalization, progress stages, opt-in generation metrics, current-page progress, cancellation, page targeting, PDF permissions, SSR-safe imports, large-document optimizations, and advanced renderer configuration.

> **Default rendering mode:** `renderMode=”canvas”`. The live playground may select another default for demonstration purposes.

#### Highlights

- Browser-side PDF generation with no package-managed upload service
- Canvas and selectable-text rendering
- Blob, ArrayBuffer, raw Base64, and PDF data-URL output
- Native browser print support in both rendering modes
- Incremental page-by-page Canvas rendering when page-break markers are present
- Cooperative cancellation for long-running exports
- Page-aware progress with `currentPage` / `totalPages`
- Opt-in total, stage, and per-page generation timing metrics
- `data-pdf-ignore` for screen-only UI that must stay out of generated PDFs
- Export-only page/body styling without mutating the visible Vue DOM
- Repeated-image caching in selectable-text rendering
- Optional TTF/TrueType-outline OTF embedding for selectable text
- Export-only chart snapshots, SVG fallback and explicit image quality controls
- Text, image and trusted HTML watermark designs with per-export reuse
- Temporary DOM/canvas cleanup between expensive rendering steps
- Password protection, owner password, PDF permission flags, metadata, and compression
- Headers, footers, logos, watermarks, page targeting, and clickable links
- SSR-safe package imports with Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4 validation
- Packed-consumer verification across npm, pnpm, Yarn, Yarn Plug’n’Play, and Bun
- Large-document stress presets from 5 through 1000 pages, plus custom counts

Presets are test inputs, not a guarantee that every page count will succeed on every device. Test representative documents in your target browsers.

> **Try it before integrating:** The live playground exposes package options, output APIs, and diagnostics interactively.

Open the interactive PDF playground
Open playground

— -

### Installation

Install the package using your preferred package manager:

```bash
npm install vue-pdf-export
# or
pnpm add vue-pdf-export
# or
yarn add vue-pdf-export
# or
bun add vue-pdf-export
```

#### Import

TypeScript:

```ts
import {
Html2Pdf,
type PdfBase64Options,
type PdfMetadataOptions,
type PdfOutputFormat,
type PdfProgressState,
type PdfRenderMode,
type PdfSecurityOptions,
type PdfSerializedOutput,
type PdfStylingOptions,
type WatermarkOptions,
} from “vue-pdf-export”;

import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;
```

JavaScript:

```js
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;
```

#### Package-manager compatibility

The packed package is validated as a consumer installation with:

- npm
- pnpm
- Yarn
- Yarn Plug’n’Play
- Bun

The compatibility fixtures verify installation, TypeScript resolution, production builds, CSS imports, and browser-side PDF generation.

#### Nuxt

`vue-pdf-export` can be imported during SSR, while PDF generation itself remains browser-only.

See Nuxt 3 & Nuxt 4 SSR for `<ClientOnly>`, lazy-import, and client-event patterns.

— -

### Quick Start

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { ref } from “vue”;
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

const pdfRef = ref<InstanceType<typeof Html2Pdf> | null>(null);

async function generatePdf() {
const blob = await pdfRef.value?.generatePdf();
console.log(blob);
}
</script>

<template>
<button type=”button” @click=”generatePdf”>Generate PDF</button>

<Html2Pdf
ref=”pdfRef”
filename=”my-report”
render-mode=”canvas”
 :manual-pagination=”true”
 :enable-download=”true”
>
<template #pdf-content>
<div>
<h1>My Report</h1>
<p>This content will be rendered into the PDF.</p>
</div>
</template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

#### Plain JavaScript with the Vue Options API

TypeScript is optional. Register `Html2Pdf` locally and call `generatePdf()` through a template ref. PDF generation runs in the browser after the component mounts.

```vue
<script>
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

export default {
components: { Html2Pdf },
methods: {
async generate() {
const blob = await this.$refs.pdf.generatePdf();
console.log(“PDF bytes:”, blob.size);
},
},
};
</script>

<template>
<button type=”button” @click=”generate”>Generate PDF</button>
<Html2Pdf ref=”pdf” :enable-download=”false”>
<template #pdf-content
><article><h1>JavaScript report</h1></article></template
>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

Without a pagination height, the renderer handles basic page flow. Set a positive `paginateElementsByHeight` when you want the smart DOM planner; see pagination. The Options API example is based on the library’s npm consumer fixture.

— -

### Rendering Modes

#### Canvas mode

Canvas mode is the default and uses the package’s existing `html2pdf.js` / `html2canvas` / `jsPDF` pipeline.

```vue
<Html2Pdf render-mode=”canvas” manual-pagination />
```

Use it when the highest possible browser CSS fidelity is more important than selectable body text.

Canvas keeps inline SVG in its export staging by default, but the final PDF page is still a raster image. Chart canvases are snapshotted on the private export clone before capture. See fonts, charts, SVG and images.

Best for:

- complex CSS
- gradients
- shadows
- transforms
- custom web fonts
- visual dashboards
- designs where browser appearance is the priority

Body content is rasterized, so normal body text is not selectable/searchable.

A viewer such as Chrome may apply OCR and let users select apparent text in an image-only PDF. A foreground text watermark or some numbering paths can also add native text over a Canvas body. Inspect PDF text operators or extract text with a PDF tool to distinguish native text from viewer OCR.

##### Incremental Canvas rendering

When the export DOM contains `.html2pdf__page-break` markers, Canvas mode uses an incremental page-by-page renderer instead of capturing the entire document as one giant canvas.

This path:

- clones and renders one logical PDF page at a time
- keeps raster dimensions page-bounded
- releases temporary page DOM after `html2canvas` finishes reading it
- releases canvas backing stores after insertion into jsPDF
- reports page-level progress
- yields to the browser between expensive steps
- supports cooperative cancellation before the next page begins

Canvas documents without page-break markers use the whole-document `html2pdf.js` worker. Paginated Canvas documents can use page-bounded incremental captures.

Oversized splittable Canvas sections are measured and re-paginated on private staging DOM before capture. Reused fitting fragments and page-by-page capture reduce repeated work; very large indivisible media can still scale or split. Vue header/footer slots use image captures in Canvas mode and supported text/shape operations in text mode.

#### Selectable text mode

```vue
<Html2Pdf render-mode=”text” manual-pagination />
```

Selectable text mode converts the live browser layout into PDF vector/text operations instead of turning the entire document into a screenshot.

In selectable-text mode, inline SVG shapes are rasterized; `svgMode=”preserve”` cannot turn them into native PDF vectors. Optional TTF or TrueType-outline OTF registration can embed a matching face for real PDF text. Without a registered font, unrecognized CSS families use built-in PDF faces.

It supports:

- selectable body text
- searchable body text
- copyable body text
- selectable header/footer text
- selectable footer page numbers
- clickable PDF hyperlinks
- images
- backgrounds
- borders
- basic border radius
- text color, weight, italic, decoration, alignment, and spacing
- multi-page output
- manual page-break markers
- PDF password protection
- PDF permissions
- metadata
- compression
- headers, footers, and watermarks

Example:

```vue
<Html2Pdf render-mode=”text” manual-pagination>

<template #pdf-content>
<main>
<h1>Selectable report</h1>
<p>You can select and search this text in the generated PDF.</p>

<a>
Open vue-pdf-export on npm
</a>
</main>
</template>
</Html2Pdf>
```

> Selectable-text mode intentionally favors real PDF text over pixel-perfect parity with every browser CSS feature. See [Selectable Text Mode Notes](#selectable-text-mode-notes).

— -

### Component Registration

#### Local import — recommended

With `<script setup>`:

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;
</script>
```

No `components` registration is required.

#### Options API

```vue
<script lang=”ts”>
import { defineComponent } from “vue”;
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

export default defineComponent({
components: {
Html2Pdf,
},
});
</script>
```

#### Global registration

```ts
import { createApp } from “vue”;
import App from “./App.vue”;
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

const app = createApp(App);

app.component(“Html2Pdf”, Html2Pdf);
app.mount(“#app”);
```

— -

### Preview & Download

Add one of these prop combinations to the complete quick-start component. Keep `manual-pagination` for a simple document, or configure a usable page-height budget for automatic pagination.

Preview only:

```vue
<Html2Pdf :enable-download=”false” :preview-modal=”true” />
```

Download only:

```vue
<Html2Pdf :enable-download=”true” :preview-modal=”false” />
```

Download and preview:

```vue
<Html2Pdf :enable-download=”true” :preview-modal=”true” />
```

`enableDownload` and `previewModal` are independent.

— -

### Smart PDF Pagination

`Html2Pdf` runs the shared DOM pagination planner when `manualPagination` is `false` and `paginateElementsByHeight` is supplied. That number is the **usable CSS pixel height after margins and header/footer reservations**, calculated for your chosen paper size and orientation. It is not a universal A4 constant. Direct `useHtml2Pdf()` generation does not run the component planner.

The component also supports a simple Options API or Composition API PDF without pagination props: the selected renderer handles basic flow. Set a positive finite height to use the smart DOM planner for keep-together rules and table rows. In the playground, manual pagination is the demo default, and the optional media/chart section has an authored break before it. A large section may continue onto another physical page. Oversized rows and unusual CSS still need PDF inspection.

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

// Example budget for this application’s measured paper geometry and insets.
const usablePageHeightPx = 960;
</script>

<template>
<Html2Pdf
 :manual-pagination=”false”
 :paginate-elements-by-height=”usablePageHeightPx”
>
<template #pdf-content>
<section data-pdf-split=”avoid”>
<h2>Summary</h2>
<p>Keep this block together if it fits.</p>
</section>
<section data-pdf-split=”container”>
<header data-pdf-split-header>Repeated section heading</header>
<article>First child</article>
<article>Second child</article>
</section>
</template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

Recalculate the budget when format, orientation, explicit margins, content width or layer heights change. The paper format guide explains geometry.

#### Split controls

| Markup | Effect |
| — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — | — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — |
| `data-pdf-split=”avoid”` | Move a fitting block together; oversized blocks can fall back to child boundaries. |
| `data-pdf-split=”container”` | Split long and nested sections around children, accounting for computed padding and flex/grid gaps. |
| `data-pdf-split-header` | Mark a child heading for repetition when its container continues. |
| `.pdf-keep-together`, `.pdf-no-break`, `img` | Existing default avoidance rules. |

In supported selectable-text layouts, continuation fragments can retain a frame with page-edge spacing and rounded borders. Renderer CSS support varies. Indivisible oversized media, rowspans and complex nested layouts may still split or scale; inspect representative exports.

#### Explicit page breaks

```html
<section style=”break-before: page”>Start on a new page.</section>
<section style=”break-after: page”>
The next block starts on a new page.
</section>
<div class=”html2pdf__page-break”></div>
```

CSS `page-break-before` and `page-break-after` are supported alongside modern break properties. Do not put an explicit CSS break on the `.html2pdf__page-break` marker: that can produce two breaks or blank pages. `manual-pagination=”true”` is useful when you author your own markers. Elements without special attributes retain their existing behavior.

#### Long tables

Use one semantic heading and ordinary rows. The planner can split across multiple `<tbody>` groups, honor explicit row breaks, move an orphan heading with its first row and repeat `<thead>` on continuation pages. Do not manually copy the heading.

```vue
<template>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th scope=”col”>Item</th>
<th scope=”col”>Amount</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr v-for=”item in 40" :key=”item”>
<td>Item {{ item }}</td>
<td>${{ item * 10 }}</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</template>
```

Selectable-text rendering carries the computed heading background into repeated rows. Canvas continuation fragments suppress a second native heading repetition. Check complex `rowspan`, unsupported CSS and oversized rows in the output.

#### Diagnose page boundaries

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import type { PdfPaginationDiagnostic } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

function onBreak(decision: PdfPaginationDiagnostic) {
console.info(decision.type, decision.page, decision.reason);
}
</script>

<template>
<Html2Pdf
 :manual-pagination=”false”
 :paginate-elements-by-height=”960"
 :pagination-debug=”true”
@pagination-break=”onBreak”
@pagination-warning=”onBreak”
@pagination-complete=”(all) => console.info(all)”
>
<template #pdf-content><article>Measured report content</article></template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

Possible diagnostic types are `automatic`, `manual-break`, `break-before`, `break-after`, `avoid-moved`, `container-split`, `table-split`, and `oversized`. The opt-in overlay and events show planner decisions on the live DOM. The overlay is not a PDF layer or proof of final viewer alignment. Pagination has a finite fallback and cancellation checks; it cannot guarantee that arbitrary text, SVG or CSS never tears.

— -

### Nuxt 3 & Nuxt 4 SSR

<p>

</p>

**Nuxt 3 + Nuxt 4 compatible**

`vue-pdf-export` supports SSR-safe package imports in both **Nuxt 3** and **Nuxt 4**. PDF generation itself uses browser APIs and must run on the client.

Validated integration paths include:

- server-side package import
- Nuxt 3 SSR build/runtime
- Nuxt 4 SSR build/runtime
- hydration
- client navigation
- lazy-loaded PDF consumers
- `<ClientOnly>` integration
- client-event composable generation

Browser-heavy PDF dependencies are loaded from generation paths instead of being eagerly evaluated during the server import path.

#### Recommended component pattern

Use `<ClientOnly>` when the export UI itself does not need to render on the server:

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { ref } from “vue”;
```

#### Lazy import on a client event

For routes where PDF functionality is only used after a user action, you can lazy-load the package from a client event:

```ts
async function loadPdfTools() {
if (!import.meta.client) return;

const pdf = await import(“vue-pdf-export”);

return pdf;
}
```

This is optional. A normal package import is SSR-safe, but lazy loading can help keep PDF-specific code out of paths that never use it.

#### Composable generation

Call browser-side generation from mounted/client UI events rather than server setup work.

```ts
import { useHtml2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;

const { generate, loading, error } = useHtml2Pdf();

async function onExportClick() {
if (!import.meta.client) return;

await generate(/* browser DOM/content options */);
}
```

#### What not to do

Do not start PDF generation while Nuxt is rendering on the server:

```ts
// Avoid server-side generation calls.
if (import.meta.server) {
// generatePdf() should not be called here.
}
```

The supported boundary is simple: **imports may happen during SSR; PDF generation happens in the browser.**

> **Nuxt compatibility:** Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4 have automated SSR import/hydration fixture coverage. Package import is SSR-safe; actual PDF generation must run in the browser.

### PDF Paper Formats and Orientation

The component accepts a named `pdf-format` string and `pdf-orientation=”portrait|landscape”` (also `p|l`). Default format is `a4`, default orientation is portrait.

```vue
<Html2Pdf pdf-format=”a3" pdf-orientation=”landscape” :manual-pagination=”true”>
<template #pdf-content><article>Landscape document</article></template>
</Html2Pdf>
```

The source normalizes A0–A10, B0–B10, C0–C10, `dl`, `letter`, `government-letter`, `legal`, `junior-legal`, `ledger`, `tabloid`, and `credit-card`. The selectable-text adapter and playground picker use these names. Small paper needs compact content; large or complex layouts still need viewer checks.

For custom dimensions, pass a numeric pair through the lower-level jsPDF options. The component’s `pdfFormat` prop is a string, so do not bind an array to `pdf-format`.

```vue
<Html2Pdf
 :manual-pagination=”true”
 :html-to-pdf-options=”{
jsPDF: { unit: ‘mm’, format: [100, 180], orientation: ‘portrait’ },
}”
>
<template #pdf-content><article>Custom-size document</article></template>
</Html2Pdf>
```

When using automatic component pagination, calculate `paginate-elements-by-height` as the usable **CSS pixel** budget for the effective format, orientation, margins and header/footer heights. The playground computes this for its selected geometry. The selectable-text A3 fractional-boundary loop fix prevents a former repeated-page hang; final visual acceptance for all combinations still needs browser inspection.

#### Permission flags

```ts
type PdfPermission = “print” | “modify” | “copy” | “annot-forms”;
```

| Permission | What it allows |
| — — — — — — — | — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — |
| `print` | Allows printing when the PDF viewer enforces document permissions. |

> PDF permission enforcement depends on the PDF viewer. Password encryption is part of the PDF itself, while permission flags rely on viewer compliance.

#### Security guidance

The package can generate encrypted/password-protected PDFs, but PDF security should be treated as one layer of application security rather than a replacement for access control.

Important boundaries:

- **User/open password** controls opening an encrypted PDF.
- **Owner password** is used by the PDF encryption layer for owner-level access/permission configuration.
- **Permission flags are viewer-dependent.** Some PDF viewers may not enforce them identically.
- Caller-supplied header, footer, and slot HTML is sanitized with DOMPurify before insertion into export staging. Supply trusted, intentional document content; sanitization is not a substitute for application security.
- Remote images are fetched by the browser. Use trusted origins, correct CORS headers, and avoid exposing secrets in image URLs.
- Passwords exist in browser memory while a PDF is being generated. Do not hard-code sensitive production passwords into public frontend source.
- Generated Blob URLs are cleaned up by the component/composable lifecycle, but applications should still avoid retaining generated Blobs longer than necessary.

`vue-pdf-export` is a client-side library and does not require a package-operated server to generate a PDF. Your application, remote assets, analytics, and surrounding infrastructure may still perform their own network requests.

#### Password parts

```ts
const security = {
enabled: true,
passwordParts: [“15081999”, 4821],
passwordSeparator: “-”,
};
```

This creates one final open password:

```text
15081999–4821
```

`passwordParts` do not create multiple independent passwords.

When `security` is omitted, compatible raw `htmlToPdfOptions.jsPDF.encryption` values are preserved.

When `security.enabled` is explicitly `false`, encryption is removed.

#### Security Model & Boundaries

`vue-pdf-export` provides PDF security features and conservative browser-side cleanup, but no client-side PDF package can make an application “100% secure” by itself.

Minifying the npm distribution is useful for package size and distribution hygiene, but it is **not** a security boundary.

The watermark controls below are available in the published package. Choose an explicit `layer` when placement matters.

```ts
mode: “repeat”,
layer: “foreground”,
imageDataUrl: logoPngDataUrl,
opacity: 0.14,
rotation: -32,
width: 20,
gapX: 5,
gapY: 5,
pages: “all”,
};
```

`imageDataUrl` supports PNG or JPEG data URLs; `imageUrl` supports a reachable URL with appropriate CORS. Width and gaps use the configured jsPDF units. The source aspect ratio determines height when omitted. `x` and `y` position a single mark; repeated marks use a grid and gaps. A transparent PNG usually gives the cleanest foreground logo. Dense repeated images are composed into a reusable transparent page sheet. Full-page PNG backgrounds can increase file size.

For a styled stamp, pass a **trusted mounted element**, for example `watermark: { enabled: true, type: ‘html’, htmlElement: stampRef.value }` after the ref exists. The element is captured as an image once per export. Do not pass an untrusted HTML string. `microtext` is visible decoration, not a digital signature or tamper protection.

Selectable-text output can draw a real background mark behind its PDF content. Canvas output has opaque raster pages and uses a light foreground fallback to keep a requested background mark visible. An opaque content card can cover a selectable-text background mark. See media and typography.

| `generatePdf({ composition? }?)` | `Promise<Blob>` | Generate the PDF and optionally override composition. |
| `generatePdfArrayBuffer()` | `Promise<ArrayBuffer>` | Generate once, then serialize the resulting Blob to binary bytes. |
| `generatePdfBase64(options?)` | `Promise<string>` | Generate once, then return raw Base64 or an optional PDF data URL. |
| `print()` | `Promise<void>` | Generate/open the native browser print flow. |
| `closePreview()` | `void` | Close the active preview flow. |

| `cancelGeneration()` | `void` | Request cooperative cancellation of active generation. |

```ts
interface Html2PdfInstance {
generatePdf: (overrides?: {
composition?: PdfCompositionOptions;
}) => Promise<Blob>;
generatePdfArrayBuffer: () => Promise<ArrayBuffer>;
generatePdfBase64: (options?: PdfBase64Options) => Promise<string>;
print: () => Promise<void>;
closePreview: () => void;
resetPagination: () => void;
cancelGeneration: () => void;
}
```

Recommended ref:

```ts
const pdfRef = ref<InstanceType<typeof Html2Pdf> | null>(null);
```

#### Generate Blob

```ts
const blob = await pdfRef.value?.generatePdf();
```

To insert existing PDF pages for this call, use `await pdfRef.value?.generatePdf({ composition: { prepend: templatePdf, append: templatePdf } })`. The method option wins over the component prop. See PDF composition.

`Blob` remains the recommended default for downloads, previews, object URLs, and very large PDFs.

#### Generate ArrayBuffer

```ts
const arrayBuffer = await pdfRef.value?.generatePdfArrayBuffer();
```

Use ArrayBuffer when you need raw PDF bytes for binary APIs, workers, storage, cryptographic processing, or transports that accept binary data.

#### Generate Base64

Raw Base64:

```ts
const base64 = await pdfRef.value?.generatePdfBase64();
```

PDF data URL:

```ts
const dataUrl = await pdfRef.value?.generatePdfBase64({
dataUrl: true,
});
```

Base64 is convenient for string-only transports, but it is larger than the binary payload and requires additional conversion memory. Prefer Blob or ArrayBuffer for large PDFs.

The ArrayBuffer and Base64 methods reuse the normal PDF generation flow and serialize the generated Blob. They do **not** run a second PDF renderer.

> For pure programmatic output, disable automatic browser-side download/preview with `:enable-download=”false”` and `:preview-modal=”false”`.

#### Low-level output serialization

The output helpers are also available directly:

```ts
import {
pdfBlobToArrayBuffer,
pdfBlobToBase64,
serializePdfOutput,
} from “vue-pdf-export”;

const bytes = await pdfBlobToArrayBuffer(blob);
const base64 = await pdfBlobToBase64(blob);
const dataUrl = await pdfBlobToBase64(blob, { dataUrl: true });

const output = await serializePdfOutput(blob, “arraybuffer”);
```

Supported output formats are `blob`, `arraybuffer`, and `base64`.

#### Print

```ts
await pdfRef.value?.print();
```

Print works through the browser print flow in both Canvas and selectable-text rendering modes.

#### Close preview

```ts
pdfRef.value?.closePreview();
```

#### Reset automatic pagination

```ts
pdfRef.value?.resetPagination();
```

This removes only automatically inserted page breaks.

#### Cancel active generation

```ts
pdfRef.value?.cancelGeneration();
```

`cancelGeneration()` requests cooperative cancellation of the current export.

- Incremental Canvas rendering checks cancellation around page capture, encoding, insertion, and browser-yield points.
- Selectable-text rendering checks cancellation while walking the DOM, materializing images, paginating, and rendering pages.
- Synchronous browser/jsPDF work such as an already-running `toDataURL()` or final `pdf.output(‘blob’)` call cannot be interrupted in the middle; cancellation takes effect at the next safe checkpoint.
- Cancellation is treated as an expected abort flow and is not emitted as the component’s normal `error` event.

### Compose Existing PDF Pages

`composition.prepend` and `composition.append` insert **whole PDF pages** before and after generated pages. They do not overlay a page. A two-page template on both sides adds four pages.

```vue

import { ref } from “vue”;
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import type { PdfCompositionOptions } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

const pdfRef = ref<InstanceType<typeof Html2Pdf> | null>(null);
const templatePdf = ref<Blob | null>(null);
const composition = ref<PdfCompositionOptions>({});

function chooseTemplate(event: Event) {
const file = (event.target as HTMLInputElement).files?.[0];
if (file) {
templatePdf.value = file;
composition.value = { prepend: file, append: file };
}
}

async function exportPdf() {
if (!templatePdf.value) return;
await pdfRef.value?.generatePdf({ composition: composition.value });
}
</script>

<template>
<input type=”file” accept=”application/pdf,.pdf” @change=”chooseTemplate” />
<button type=”button” :disabled=”!templatePdf” @click=”exportPdf”>
Export combined PDF
</button>
<Html2Pdf
ref=”pdfRef”
 :manual-pagination=”true”
 :enable-download=”true”
 :composition=”composition”
>
<template #pdf-content><article>Generated document</article></template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

`PdfTemplateSource` accepts `Blob`, `ArrayBuffer`, `Uint8Array`, or a URL string pointing to a real PDF. Browser `fetch()` of remote URLs needs CORS access. Password-protected template PDFs may not load; verify the source before export. The same source used twice is resolved once per generation. The composition engine loads only when needed.

Method `generatePdf({ composition })` takes precedence over the `composition` prop. The object prop takes precedence over the convenience pair `pdf-template` and `template-position=”prepend|append|both”`; that pair defaults to prepend. Composition can also be passed through the lower-level options. Generated headers, footers, watermarks, and `{total}` are applied before inserted pages, so their page numbering excludes templates. Cancellation is checked around fetch, parsing, and serialization. The implementation reapplies metadata and encryption to the combined output when configured, but test the resulting permissions and metadata in your target viewers.

For Blob/ArrayBuffer/Base64 output, see the programmatic API. The playground offers composition upload and page-order checks.

### Selectable Text Mode

Selectable-text mode uses a browser-layout-to-vector-PDF renderer rather than html2canvas for the main body content.

#### How do I generate a searchable PDF in Vue 3?

Install `vue-pdf-export`, import `Html2Pdf` and its stylesheet, set `render-mode=”text”`, then call `generatePdf()` from a component ref after the Vue component mounts. The returned value is a PDF `Blob`; with `enable-download` enabled, the component can also download it. This example uses the current documented package API.

```bash
npm install vue-pdf-export
```

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { ref } from “vue”;
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

const pdf = ref<InstanceType<typeof Html2Pdf> | null>(null);

async function downloadReport() {
const blob = await pdf.value?.generatePdf();
if (blob) console.log(`Generated ${blob.size} PDF bytes`);
}
</script>

<template>
<button type=”button” @click=”downloadReport”>Download searchable PDF</button>
<Html2Pdf
ref=”pdf”
render-mode=”text”
filename=”searchable-report.pdf”
 :enable-download=”true”
>
<template #pdf-content>
<article>
<h1>Monthly report</h1>
<p>This body text is selectable and searchable.</p>
</article>
</template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

The PDF body text can be selected, copied, and searched in a compatible viewer. Test the result with your fonts and browser: not every CSS effect or glyph has a native-text equivalent. In Nuxt, follow the SSR guide and start generation only in the browser.

#### Vue PDF export: which renderer should I use?

Use `renderMode=”canvas”` when matching complex browser CSS matters most. It uses the html2pdf.js / html2canvas / jsPDF path, so PDF body text is drawn as an image. Use `renderMode=”text”` when users need to select, search or copy body text in the PDF. Both modes work through the same Vue component and support preview, download and Blob output. Start with the Vue quick start, then compare rendering modes.

The package adds Vue components, typed options, slots and pagination controls around these workflows. Selectable-text mode has its own CSS limits below; it is not a pixel-for-pixel replacement for the Canvas path.

#### What it is designed to preserve

- real PDF text
- selection/search/copy
- text line placement based on browser layout
- common font weight/style/color/alignment
- backgrounds
- borders
- images
- opacity
- overflow clipping
- multi-page layout
- clickable links

#### Current limitations

Some browser CSS/features are not fully reproduced in selectable-text mode, including or depending on renderer support:

- complex stacking-context / `z-index` reordering
- background images and gradients
- shadows
- CSS transforms
- CFF-outline OTF and WOFF/WOFF2 embedding (registered TTF and TrueType-outline OTF are supported)
- some non-WinAnsi glyphs such as CJK/emoji
- pseudo-elements such as `::before` / `::after`
- native list markers in some layouts
- RTL text
- `position: fixed`
- complex rounded clipping
- native `break-inside: avoid` semantics inside the vector renderer

For those cases, prefer `renderMode=”canvas”`.

The `fonts` option can register TTF or TrueType-outline OTF files for selectable text. Without a registered file, unrecognized CSS font families map to built-in PDF fonts. Inline SVG shapes are rasterized in this mode. See fonts, charts, SVG and images.

#### Font metric differences

Selectable text uses PDF font metrics, which can differ slightly from browser web-font metrics. Most normal text is visually close, but highly stylized button/link text with large letter spacing or fixed widths can look different.

#### Header/footer text

In selectable-text mode, plain header/footer text and footer page-number text are emitted as real selectable PDF text. Complex HTML styling may be simplified to preserve selectability.

#### Security

Selectable-text mode supports PDF encryption because the vendored vector renderer passes the package’s jsPDF constructor options at document creation time.

#### Rendering modes reference

#### Canvas mode

Canvas mode is the default and uses the package’s existing `html2pdf.js` / `html2canvas` / `jsPDF` pipeline.

```vue
<Html2Pdf render-mode=”canvas” />
```

Use it when the highest possible browser CSS fidelity is more important than selectable body text.

Best for:

- complex CSS
- gradients
- shadows
- transforms
- custom web fonts
- visual dashboards
- designs where browser appearance is the priority

Body content is rasterized, so normal body text is not selectable/searchable.

##### Incremental Canvas rendering

When the export DOM contains `.html2pdf__page-break` markers, Canvas mode uses an incremental page-by-page renderer instead of capturing the entire document as one giant canvas.

This path:

- clones and renders one logical PDF page at a time
- keeps raster dimensions page-bounded
- releases temporary page DOM after `html2canvas` finishes reading it
- releases canvas backing stores after insertion into jsPDF
- reports page-level progress
- yields to the browser between expensive steps
- supports cooperative cancellation before the next page begins

Canvas documents without page-break markers use the whole-document `html2pdf.js` worker; paginated documents can use incremental page captures.

#### Selectable text mode

```vue
<Html2Pdf render-mode=”text” />
```

Selectable text mode converts the live browser layout into PDF vector/text operations instead of turning the entire document into a screenshot.

It supports:

- selectable body text
- searchable body text
- copyable body text
- selectable header/footer text
- selectable footer page numbers
- clickable PDF hyperlinks
- images
- backgrounds
- borders
- basic border radius
- text color, weight, italic, decoration, alignment, and spacing
- multi-page output
- manual page-break markers
- PDF password protection
- PDF permissions
- metadata
- compression
- headers, footers, and watermarks

Example:

```vue

<p>You can select and search this text in the generated PDF.</p>

Open vue-pdf-export on npm
```

Remote images must be accessible to the browser during rendering.

Recommended:

```ts
html2canvas: {
useCORS: true,
}
```

For external images:

- configure appropriate CORS headers
- avoid inaccessible authenticated image URLs
- prefer data URLs for critical logos when practical
- preserve image aspect ratio

Normal content image CSS:

```css
.pdf-root img {
max-width: 100%;
height: auto;
object-fit: contain;
}
```

Header/footer logo sizing is already aspect-ratio-safe internally. Their width and height props define maximum bounds instead of forced image dimensions.

#### Image optimization

Opt-in `autoOptimize` provides target DPI, JPEG quality, alpha preservation, size caps, and per-export repeated-image reuse. Existing library image quality remains unchanged when it is disabled. A cross-origin image that cannot be decoded is left unchanged and may still be subject to the renderer’s CORS restrictions.

### Production Guide

#### Use a deterministic export width

A PDF should not unexpectedly reflow because it was generated from a narrow mobile viewport.

```css
.pdf-root {
width: 794px;
box-sizing: border-box;
}
```

#### Keep export CSS separate from responsive application CSS

The web UI and the PDF document have different layout goals.

#### Choose the renderer intentionally

Use `canvas` when exact visual fidelity is the priority.

Use `text` when selectable/searchable/copyable PDF text is the priority and the document uses CSS supported by the vector renderer.

#### Avoid large fixed heights

Prefer `min-height` over large fixed `height` values where possible.

#### Protect important blocks

Use `.pdf-keep-together`, `.pdf-no-break`, or carefully chosen `pagebreak.avoid` selectors.

#### Preserve image aspect ratios

```css
img {
max-width: 100%;
height: auto;
object-fit: contain;
}
```

#### Keep header/footer content inside configured heights

Very large text or HTML content can overlap PDF content if it exceeds `headerHeight` or `footerHeight`.

#### Use trusted HTML only

`headerHtml` and `footerHtml` render developer-provided HTML. Header, footer, and slot HTML is sanitized with DOMPurify before export staging. Supply intentional, trusted document markup; sanitization does not turn arbitrary input into trusted application content.

#### Test fonts and media on the target browser

Wait for project fonts and register supported font bytes when exact selectable-text glyphs matter. Keep `autoOptimize` opt-in and choose DPI/JPEG quality appropriate to your output. Test SVG icons, chart snapshots, and font fallback in your target browsers.

#### Keep selectable-mode link styles simple

Avoid excessive letter spacing, transforms, or tightly fixed widths for PDF links/buttons when using selectable-text mode.

#### Use reasonable canvas quality

Higher html2canvas scale values consume more memory and CPU.

#### Generate one large document at a time

Multi-page PDF generation can be CPU and memory intensive.

#### Provide cancellation for expensive exports

Expose `cancelGeneration()` in long-running workflows so users can stop an export without waiting for the entire document to finish.

Cancellation is cooperative: already-running synchronous browser/jsPDF work finishes before the next cancellation checkpoint.

Large client-side PDF generation is constrained by browser memory, canvas limits, image size, document complexity, encryption overhead, and the device running the page. The package therefore uses multiple strategies rather than assuming one renderer is safe for every document.

The architectural changes behind these results include:

- rendering static HTML footers once and reusing them across pages

- releasing temporary DOM and canvas backing stores earlier
- caching repeated selectable-mode images within one generation
- yielding between expensive rendering steps
- adding cancellation and page-aware progress

#### Incremental Canvas strategy

For Canvas documents with `.html2pdf__page-break` markers, each logical page is rendered independently.

This avoids the old failure mode where a long document could become one extremely tall browser canvas. In regression testing, the incremental path restored correct 50-page and 100-page Canvas PDF output while keeping individual captures page-bounded.

The whole-document `html2pdf.js` path is used for Canvas documents without page-break markers.

#### Selectable-text image optimization

Selectable-text rendering uses a **per-generation image cache** for repeated real `<img>` sources when the source, target raster dimensions, format, and JPEG quality match.

Why the cache is intentionally per-generation:

- avoids carrying stale DOM/image state across exports
- keeps cache lifetime bounded
- prevents a global cache from becoming a long-lived memory owner

Canvas elements are not cached because their pixels may change even when their dimensions do not.

#### Cleanup and browser responsiveness

Long exports explicitly release temporary resources where practical:

- off-screen incremental page DOM is removed after `html2canvas` no longer needs it
- temporary canvas backing stores are reset after serialization/insertion
- selectable image-materialization canvases are released after encoding
- per-generation image caches are cleared after use
- rendering loops periodically yield with browser scheduling checkpoints

Yielding does not make CPU-heavy work free, but it gives the browser opportunities to process progress updates and cancellation rather than monopolizing the main thread for the entire export.

#### Cancellation and recovery

Both rendering modes support cooperative cancellation.

The regression suite checks that:

1. an active long export can be cancelled,
2. temporary rendering DOM is cleaned up,
3. no successful Blob is exposed for the cancelled run, and
4. a new PDF can be generated successfully afterwards.

#### Page progress

Page-aware renderers can report:

```ts
{
stage: ‘rendering’,
progress: number,
currentPage?: number,
totalPages?: number,
}
```

This is useful for long reports where a percentage alone does not explain what the renderer is doing.

#### Encrypted Canvas memory behavior

Large encrypted Canvas PDFs can retain substantially more memory than equivalent unencrypted Canvas PDFs in Chromium.

Isolation testing reproduced the severe encrypted-raster retention pattern with raw jsPDF usage, outside the Vue component lifecycle. For that reason this is tracked as an upstream/dependency concern rather than described as a confirmed Vue memory leak.

Practical guidance:

- avoid unnecessarily high Canvas scale values
- resize oversized images before PDF generation
- generate one very large document at a time
- prefer selectable-text mode when it meets the document’s visual requirements
- test encrypted long documents on representative target devices
- consider splitting exceptionally large documents when browser memory is constrained

> **Upstream jsPDF tracking**: large encrypted Canvas PDFs can show substantially higher memory retention than equivalent unencrypted Canvas PDFs in Chromium. The same encrypted-raster pattern was reproduced in a raw jsPDF-only test outside the Vue component lifecycle, so this is tracked as an upstream/dependency concern rather than described as a confirmed Vue memory leak. See jsPDF issue #4017.

### Troubleshooting

#### Selectable text is not pixel-identical to the browser

Use `render-mode=”canvas”` for maximum CSS fidelity.

Selectable-text mode intentionally prioritizes real PDF text and vector output.

#### Link looks like text but is not clickable

Make sure links are enabled:

```ts
const htmlToPdfOptions = {
enableLinks: true,
};
```

Also verify the source element is a real anchor with a valid `href`.

#### Link text looks stretched

Reduce large `letter-spacing`, transforms, and tight fixed widths in selectable-text mode.

#### Logo looks stretched

Header/footer logo dimensions are maximum bounds and preserve the source aspect ratio.

For normal content images:

```css
img {
width: auto;
height: auto;
max-width: 100%;
object-fit: contain;
}
```

#### Header/footer overlaps content

Increase `headerHeight` / `footerHeight`, or reduce content size.

For selectively targeted headers, only target pages receive the extra header space. If excluded pages still have top spacing, check explicit `htmlToPdfOptions.margin`.

#### Header or footer image is missing

Check:

- URL accessibility
- CORS
- data URL validity
- `headerLogoEnabled`
- `footerLogoEnabled`

A large source logo displayed at a small size is capped to a proportional raster size during selectable-text header/footer preparation. The source file and caller options remain unchanged.

#### HTML header/footer is not visible

Check that:

- related header/footer is enabled
- HTML string is non-empty
- footer uses `footer-mode=”html”`
- content fits inside configured height

#### Blank page around a manual break

Use only:

```css
.html2pdf__page-break {
display: block;
height: 0;
clear: both;
}
```

Do not add `break-before` or `page-break-before` to the same helper.

#### Background watermark is hidden

Opaque PDF content can cover a DOM background watermark.

In selectable-text mode, a requested background watermark is drawn behind PDF content, but opaque cards can cover it. Canvas pages are opaque images, so a requested background mark uses a light foreground fallback to remain visible.

#### PDF is blurry

In canvas mode, increase `pdfQuality` or `htmlToPdfOptions.html2canvas.scale` carefully.

Selectable-text body text remains vector text and does not depend on html2canvas resolution.

#### Large document generation is slow

Reduce:

- canvas scale where relevant
- image dimensions
- document complexity
- simultaneous PDF generation

Large encrypted Canvas PDFs can show substantially higher memory retention than unencrypted Canvas PDFs in Chromium. Raw jsPDF-only isolation reproduced the same encrypted-raster retention pattern outside the Vue lifecycle, so this is tracked as an upstream/dependency concern rather than described as a confirmed permanent Vue memory leak. Selectable-text mode did not show the same severe raster-memory pattern in the package benchmarks.

#### A header or footer appears empty

The component accepts direct props as well as `header` and `footer` objects. Explicit object fields take priority, while omitted fields may fall back to matching direct props. Check the enabled flag, slot content, object settings, and reserved height. For a new integration, prefer the grouped object API or Vue slots.

#### Table heading repeats twice, or a row crosses a page cut

Use one semantic `<thead>` and normal `<tbody>` rows. Avoid manually duplicated headings. Try smart pagination and its diagnostic overlay. Large rowspans, oversized rows and unusual CSS need manual review in both renderers.

#### Canvas PDF appears to have selectable text

Chrome can OCR page images. Foreground text watermarks or some numbering paths may also add native text. Inspect extracted PDF text or text-showing operators rather than relying only on mouse selection. Use `render-mode=”text”` for native selectable body text.

### Performance Engineering

The large-document milestone was not only a benchmark exercise. It changed the runtime architecture and added repeatable correctness, cleanup and memory diagnostics.

> The measurements below are historical fixtures. The latest full browser and stress reruns were not part of this docs update; measure your own document on target devices.

#### Rendering architecture

The package dynamically loads PDF engines and the optional composition engine, resolves a shared template once, reuses unchanged header/footer and styled slot captures, reduces repeated image waiting, and prunes unrelated app DOM while capturing a layer. Oversized splittable Canvas sections are preflight paginated on private DOM, then fitting fragments are reused. Cooperative yields avoid waiting for hidden-tab animation frames. Generation reuses one final Blob for preview and download, with cleanup, cancellation and opt-in timing metrics.

A local nine-page Canvas/slot export with watermark off was inspected: 27 image objects and zero PDF text-showing commands; a separate text-mode PDF contained 423 text commands. One local Canvas slot session changed from 26.89 seconds to 12.55 seconds after the refinements, without a controlled benchmark. A separate nine-page text run was about 4.35 seconds; no text-mode speedup was established. These observations do not predict your document’s runtime or fidelity. Record browser/device, page count, renderer, assets, quality and cold/warm state when comparing exports.

#### Executive outcome

- paginated Canvas documents can render page by page instead of one giant document-height canvas
- 50-page and 100-page Canvas exports are verified as real, non-empty PDFs on the incremental path
- static HTML footer content is rasterized once and reused across pages
- selectable-text mode caches repeated image sources within one generation
- long work can be cancelled and then safely regenerated
- progress can expose `stage`, `progress`, `currentPage` and `totalPages`
- temporary DOM, Canvas backing stores and encoded image references are released earlier
- browser yielding was added between expensive chunks

### Fonts, Charts, SVG and Image Optimization

The following media controls are part of the published `vue-pdf-export` API. Use the current official reference when integrating them.

`vue-pdf-export` generates PDFs in the browser from Vue 3 content. It prepares media in a private export clone: it waits for fonts, snapshots chart canvases, applies the SVG policy and optionally optimizes images. The live Vue page stays intact, and temporary DOM, font registrations and caches are cleaned after completion, failure or cancellation.

#### Configure media for a Vue PDF

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import type {
PdfFontSource,
PdfImageOptimizationOptions,
} from “vue-pdf-export”;

const fonts: PdfFontSource[] = [
{
family: “Report Sans”,
source: “/fonts/report-sans.ttf”,
format: “ttf”,
weight: 400,
},
];
const autoOptimize: PdfImageOptimizationOptions = {
targetDpi: 144,
jpegQuality: 0.85,
preserveAlpha: true,
cacheRepeated: true,
};
</script>

<template>
<Html2Pdf
render-mode=”text”
 :fonts=”fonts”
 :auto-optimize=”autoOptimize”
svg-mode=”auto”
>
<template #pdf-content><article>Report content</article></template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

`fonts`, `autoOptimize` and `svgMode` can also be passed through `htmlToPdfOptions`. Explicit component props win. `autoOptimize` is off unless you enable it, so existing image quality stays as configured.

#### Custom fonts and selectable PDF text

Export waits for `document.fonts.ready` before layout. With no custom `fonts` list, Canvas uses the page’s computed CSS font. Selectable-text mode still measures the CSS layout but maps unregistered font families to built-in PDF faces. Register a matching file when the exact project font must appear as selectable text.

Each `PdfFontSource` takes `family`, optional `style` (`normal` or `italic`), optional `weight`, `source` (URL, `ArrayBuffer` or `Uint8Array`), and optional `format` (`ttf` or `otf`). The CSS `font-family` must match `family`. Register the bold and italic files separately if the document uses them. The supported OTF path requires TrueType outlines; CFF-outline OTF, WOFF and WOFF2 cannot be embedded by this path. Remote URLs need working CORS, CSP and permission to use the font. Test the actual glyphs and language in a PDF viewer because shaping remains renderer-dependent.

#### Canvas charts and inline SVG

Canvas charts are captured as export-only PNG snapshots. Static numeric labels and fixed callouts can be present in the PDF; live hover tooltips cannot remain interactive in a static document. The four-chart ApexCharts sample is **playground-only** and does not add ApexCharts to the library’s runtime requirements.

| `svgMode` | Canvas PDF | Selectable-text PDF |
| — — — — — — — — | — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — | — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — |
| `auto` (default) | Keep inline SVG in staging; the final page is rasterized | Rasterize SVG because the text renderer does not draw SVG shapes |
| `preserve` | Keep inline SVG in staging | Rasterize unsupported SVG shapes |
| `rasterize` | Snapshot SVG into an image first | Rasterize SVG |

External SVG resources, filters, animation and `foreignObject` can differ from the live browser. Test representative charts, logos and icons in both rendering modes.

#### Image quality and per-export reuse

With `autoOptimize`, oversized raster images are downscaled from their displayed size and `targetDpi` (default 144). `maxWidth` and `maxHeight` cap output dimensions. `jpegQuality` defaults to 0.85 and is limited to 0.1–1. `preserveAlpha` defaults to `true`, choosing PNG for suitable non-JPEG sources; setting it to `false` flattens transparency onto white for JPEG. `cacheRepeated` defaults to `true` and reuses matching prepared sources, dimensions, format and quality during one export. Selectable-text rendering also has its own per-render image cache. Canvas pages remain raster page images, so object-level reuse is different.

Repeated image watermarks reuse the prepared source within one export. Sparse layouts reuse a PDF image alias; dense tiled layouts reuse one transparent sheet per page size. Static Canvas footer HTML and unchanged slot captures also reuse preparation. Set `collectMetrics` to inspect `metrics.media` operation counts, including chart snapshots, SVG rasterizations, optimized images, cache hits, watermark reuse and footer captures. These counters are not a speed or byte-saving guarantee. See watermarks and performance engineering.

#### CORS, failure and cleanup

Use same-origin media, a server that permits the page origin through CORS, or suitable data URLs. If image optimization cannot decode a cross-origin image, it leaves the staging image in place and warns; the renderer may still fail under its own CORS policy. A CORS-tainted watermark raises an error. Remote fonts can also fail during fetch. Private staging and temporary font registrations are cleaned on success, error and cancellation. See images and CORS for recovery steps.

#### Media, pagination and cleanup improvements

- Selectable-text table continuation now places an automatic split and repeated heading before the first row that crowds a measured page boundary. The inspected playground fixture no longer has a row-only page at that boundary. Oversized indivisible cells remain a limit.
- A large source logo used at a small header/footer size is rasterized proportionally for selectable-text output. A local nine-page fixture shrank from about 973 KB to about 300 KB; other documents can differ.
- Canvas page encoding uses `toBlob` and binary bytes where available, with a data-URL fallback. The playground’s JPEG quality was set to 0.88 in the measured demo configuration; that setting is not a library default.
- Export HTML paths for headers, footers and slots are sanitized before staging insertion. A cancelled preflight and late-result guard prevent a cancelled generation from opening a completed preview.

See pagination, security and project flow for their boundaries.

The library’s media verification records unit, TypeScript and build checks, Chromium and WebKit exports, and selected visual PDF inspections. Local Firefox verification failed at the headless graphics launch and remains open. Later pagination and footer fixes have narrower checks. These results cover named fixtures, not arbitrary HTML/CSS or a universal speed target. The testing guide explains how to verify your own content.

### PDF Generation Flow

`vue-pdf-export` exposes an `Html2Pdf` component and a `useHtml2Pdf` composable. The component coordinates props, slots, pagination, preview and download. The composable manages generation state, progress, cancellation and output URLs. The core prepares content and chooses a renderer; renderer modules own Canvas or selectable-text output.

#### From Vue content to PDF Blob

1. The component resolves options and, when a positive pagination height is supplied, plans DOM page breaks. Direct composable calls provide their own prepared element and page breaks.
2. Core creates a private export staging clone, applies export-only styles and ignore markers, waits for fonts and images, and prepares chart, SVG and image assets. The live Vue page is left alone.
3. Selectable-text mode maps supported DOM text, shapes, images and links into PDF operations. Canvas mode captures page images, one page at a time when markers are available, or uses its classic html2pdf path otherwise.
4. Page styling, watermarks, headers, footers, metadata, optional page composition and security are applied to the PDF.
5. One serialized Blob feeds preview, download, print or output conversion. Cleanup releases staging content, temporary fonts and media caches; the UI later revokes its owned Blob URLs.

The public library defaults to Canvas. The playground can use its own demo defaults. Nuxt imports are SSR safe, but PDF generation needs a browser DOM. See rendering modes, pagination, media preparation and programmatic output.

### Vue to PDF in Vue 3 and Nuxt

To turn a Vue component into a PDF in the browser, install `vue-pdf-export`, put the document inside its `#pdf-content` slot, and call `generatePdf()` from a component ref. Choose Canvas rendering when visual CSS fidelity matters most, or selectable-text rendering when people must search and copy body text.

#### Generate a PDF from a Vue component

```vue
<script setup lang=”ts”>
import { ref } from “vue”;
import { Html2Pdf } from “vue-pdf-export”;
import “vue-pdf-export/style.css”;

const pdf = ref<InstanceType<typeof Html2Pdf> | null>(null);

async function downloadReport() {
await pdf.value?.generatePdf();
}
</script>

<template>
<button type=”button” @click=”downloadReport”>Download report</button>
<Html2Pdf ref=”pdf” filename=”report.pdf” render-mode=”canvas”>
<template #pdf-content>
<article>
<h1>Report</h1>
<p>Rendered from a Vue component.</p>
</article>
</template>
</Html2Pdf>
</template>
```

The package’s default is Canvas. The explicit `render-mode` above makes the choice visible. For a JavaScript Options API example and download settings, use the quick start. For Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4, import the component safely during SSR and generate only after the browser mounts; see the Nuxt guide.

| Match browser CSS, charts and visual reports | Canvas mode | The page body becomes an image; readers cannot select its text. |
| Search, select or copy report text | Selectable-text mode | Some CSS, glyph and SVG behavior differs from the browser; test the actual document. |
| Print an entire server-rendered route without a browser user action | A server browser such as Playwright `page.pdf()` in an appropriate Nuxt server route | You operate a browser service and handle its server resources and access controls. |

The html2pdf.js project documents that its Canvas path renders content as an image, so text is not searchable or selectable. `vue-pdf-export` exposes that style of capture as its Canvas mode and also provides a selectable-text renderer. These modes share the component API, pagination controls, preview, download and print flow.

#### Can Vue-generated PDFs be searched?

Yes, when you use `render-mode=”text”` for the document body. PDF viewers can then select and search the emitted text. Canvas mode keeps the body as page images. Custom TTF or TrueType-outline OTF files can be registered for selectable text; CFF-outline OTF and WOFF/WOFF2 are not supported for embedding. See fonts, charts, SVG and images for the renderer-specific limits.

#### Can I combine PDFs in Vue?

You can prepend or append existing PDF pages to a generated document using the published composition options. This combines whole pages; it does not provide arbitrary editing of their internal content.

#### What should I test before shipping?

Export a representative document in each target browser. Check page breaks, font loading, remote-image CORS, output size, links and text selection as applicable. For long reports, use page-aware progress, cancellation and generation metrics and test a realistic page count. The production guide covers release checks.

A expectativa é de um “sold out” em breve, com a participação de 12 mil atletas já confirmados e um limite de até 17 mil, incluindo corredores de 20 países diferentes. A prova, que acontece em um único dia, deve ser dividida em dois dias a partir de 2027 para acomodar mais participantes.
